lessons.title: Text in Variables
intro: FORTRAN was made for numbers, and early FORTRAN had no type for text. Programmers stored letters in INTEGER variables: on the IBM System/360, one INTEGER word holds 4 characters.

In a DATA statement, 4HFORT is a Hollerith constant: 4 characters, F, O, R, T. The H is for Herman Hollerith, who invented punched cards for the 1890 US census. FORTRAN IV also allowed quotes: 'FORT'.
To print text from a variable, FORMAT has the A code: A4 prints the 4 characters. An array of words holds a longer text.

exercises.prompt: How many characters does one INTEGER word hold on the System/360?
exercises.explanation: 4 bytes, one character each. (The older IBM 7090 fit 6 characters in its 36-bit words.)

options: A Hollerith constant: the 5 characters HELLO
exercises.explanation: The count comes first, then H, then exactly that many characters.
A is the format code for text in variables.

exercises.prompt: Who is the H in Hollerith constants named after?
options: Herman Hollerith, inventor of the punched card machines
exercises.explanation: His company later became part of IBM.
A4 turns the stored characters back into text.

exercises.prompt: Why did programmers use INTEGER variables for text?
options: Early FORTRAN had no type for text

lessons.title: Reading Text Cards
intro: The A format reads text, too. READ (5,10) WORD with 10 FORMAT (A4) takes the next 4 columns of the card as characters.
To read a whole line of text, read an array: 20A4 fills 20 words, 80 columns: a whole punched card.
One character per word is handy for working letter by letter: 80A1 puts each column into its own array element, filled up with blanks.

exercises.prompt: How many columns does FORMAT (A4) read?
exercises.explanation: The number after A is the width.

exercises.prompt: How many words do you need for a whole 80-column card with A4?
Read one character into each element of C.
What does this deck print, with the data card HELLO?
exercises.explanation: The implied DO loop goes from 5 down to 1.

exercises.prompt: What's in C(9) and C(10) when the card only has 8 characters?
exercises.explanation: A short card counts as blank columns.

exercises.prompt: Why read letters one per word with A1?
options: To work with each letter on its own
exercises.explanation: Counting, comparing or reversing letters is easy then.

lessons.title: Comparing Text
intro: Text in variables can be compared with .EQ.: the same characters give the same stored number. To find all the E's on a card, compare each letter with a variable that holds E.
That's why DATA statements full of single letters, like DATA BLANK /1H /, E /1HE/, were at the top of many FORTRAN programs.
The letters are also stored in alphabetical order as numbers, so .LT. can sort names too.

code: IF (C(I) .NE. BLANK .AND. C(I - 1) .EQ. BLANK) NW = NW + 1
inputs: THERE ARE THREE E WORDS HERE

exercises.prompt: How do you check if C(I) is the letter A?
options: Compare it with a variable that holds A: IF (C(I) .EQ. LA)
exercises.explanation: In FORTRAN IV, letters are compared through variables filled by DATA.

exercises.prompt: Why does DATA BLANK /1H / appear in so many old programs?
options: To compare letters with a blank, for example to find words
exercises.explanation: A new word starts where a blank is followed by a letter.
Here LS holds the letter, from DATA LS /1HS/.

exercises.prompt: What does this deck print, with the data card ABBA?
exercises.explanation: Two of the four letters are B.

exercises.prompt: Can text in INTEGER variables be sorted with .LT.?
options: Yes: the letters are stored in alphabetical order as numbers
exercises.explanation: A has a smaller code than B, so ADA .LT. KEN.

exercises.prompt: Which FORTRAN version finally added a CHARACTER type?
exercises.explanation: With CHARACTER*20 NAME and real string operations.
